evals.prompt: Define semiotics for interface design and distinguish signifier from signified.
expected_elements: Defines semiotics as analysis of sign systems rather than aesthetic taste
Names signifiers as perceivable forms such as icons, colors, shapes, words, or interaction cues
Names signifieds as the concepts, states, actions, or judgments those forms point to
Explains that interfaces communicate through multiple sign channels at once
Mentions that the goal is coherent intended meaning for users

evals.prompt: Use Peirce, Saussure, Barthes, and Norman to analyze a warning badge that combines a triangle icon, yellow color, and the word Review.
expected_elements: Classifies the triangle/icon channel using icon/index/symbol reasoning
Separates signifier from signified
Separates literal denotation from connotation or judgment
Uses signifier/affordance language for the action expectation created by the badge
Checks whether all channels point to the same intended state or action

evals.prompt: A product team says users misread a dashboard because green means both revenue went up and costs went up. Explain the semiotic problem and the purpose of fixing it.
expected_elements: Identifies a denotation/connotation conflict
Separates direction of change from business judgment
Explains that color is already communicating whether intended or not
Recommends pairing color with text, icon, shape, or another sign channel
Frames the fix as preserving user trust and reducing misread inference

evals.prompt: Distinguish semiotics from microcopy, visual-design-foundations, a11y, semantics, semantic-relations, linguistics, and ontology-modeling.
expected_elements: microcopy owns the exact UI wording
visual-design-foundations owns craft choices such as palette, typography, spacing, and hierarchy
a11y owns accessibility compliance such as contrast and non-color alternatives
semantics owns meaning encoded in individual textual identifiers/signals
semantic-relations owns typed concept-to-concept relations
linguistics owns word-form and language-structure questions
ontology-modeling owns formal class and what-exists models
semiotics owns sign-to-meaning analysis across interface sign systems

evals.prompt: Classify common UI sign failures into icon polysemy, opacity, cultural collision, color-only state signaling, misleading affordance, and vague code/API signifiers.
expected_elements: Icon polysemy means one icon maps to multiple meanings in the product or across conventions
Opacity means the sign has no clear signified without explanation
Cultural collision means the metaphor fails for part of the audience
Color-only state signaling relies on hue as the only meaningful channel
Misleading affordance means the perceived action cue does not match actual actionability
Vague code/API signifiers force readers to inspect implementation before understanding intent

evals.prompt: Explain semiotics with an analogy that preserves the idea that words, icons, position, color, and interaction cues communicate together.
expected_elements: Uses a multi-channel communication analogy
Preserves that signs work together as a system
Shows that changing one cue can change meaning even if words stay the same
Explains user interpretation rather than designer taste
Does not collapse semiotics into copywriting or visual polish

evals.prompt: Audit a disabled button that only becomes pale gray but still has hover styling and sits in the primary-action position of a dialog.
expected_elements: Identifies a weak or conflicting anti-affordance
Notes that hover styling and primary placement still signify actionability
Recommends removing interactive signifiers or adding clearer disabled cues
Mentions that color alone is not a sufficient state signal
Checks whether text/icon/shape/state cues agree with disabled behavior

evals.prompt: A designer says icon confusion is just subjective taste and users will learn the icon over time. Correct the misconception.
expected_elements: Rejects the idea that sign-system failures are merely taste
Explains that ambiguous icons impose inference cost and reduce trust
Mentions that only a few icons are widely recognized without labels
Recommends text pairing, convention alignment, or user testing for unfamiliar icons
Distinguishes learned convention from assuming meaning will emerge automatically
